statement.p: Suppose C is the line segment from the point (0,0) to the point (3,24) and \vec{F}=xy\,\vec i + 3x\,\vec j.

(a) Is \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} greater than, less than, or equal to zero?
?
greater than zero
less than zero
equal to zero

p.em: (Be sure you are able to give a geometric explanation for your answer.)

statement.p: (b) A parameterization of C is (x(t),y(t)) = (t,8 t) for 0 \leq t \leq 3. Use this to compute \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}.

(c) Suppose a particle leaves the point (0,0), moves along the line toward the point (3,24), stops before reaching it and backs up, stops again and reverses direction, then completes its journey to the endpoint. All travel takes place along the line segment joining the point (0,0) to the point (3,24). Call this path C'. How is \int_{C'} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} related to \int_{C} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r}?

p.em: (Be sure you can explain why this is.)

statement.p: (d) A parameterization for a path like C' is given by (x(t),y(t)) = \left(\frac{1}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right), \frac{8}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right))\right). For what value of t is this parameterization
(Enter your equation in terms of x and y: thus, if y(t) = 3 x(t)^2 - 6, you would enter y = 3x^2 - 6.).
By hand, on a separate sheet of paper, verify that this equation is in fact satisfied by this parameterization.
At what values of t does the particle change direction?
(e) Set up and find \int_{C'} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} using the parameterization in part (d).

p.em: (Note whether you get the same answer as you did in part (b).)

static.solution:
(a) The line integral \int_C (1 xy\,\vec i + 3 x\,\vec j) \cdot d\vec{r} is greater than zero. This follows from the fact that all of the vectors of 1 xy\,\vec i + 3 x\,\vec j at points along C point approximately in the same direction as C (meaning the angles between the vectors and the direction of C are less than \pi/2).
(b) Using the parameterization x(t)=t, y(t)=8 t, with x'(t)=1, y'(t)=8, we have \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_0^{3} \vec{F}(t,8 t) \cdot (\vec i + 3\vec j)\,dt = \int_0^{3} (8 t^2\vec i + 3 t\vec j) \cdot (\vec i + 8\vec j)\,dt. Expanding the dot product and integrating, we have \int_C \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_0^{3} (8 t^2 + 24 t) \,dt = \left(\frac{8}{3} t^3 + 12 t^2\right) \bigg|_0^{3} = 180.
(c) Call the point on the oriented path C' where the particle stops and reverses direction P and the point where it changes direction again Q. Then we can view C' as a sum of three paths: C_1, on which the particle moves from (0,0) along the line connecting (0,0) and (3,24) until it gets to the point P; C_2, the path connecting the point P and the point Q; and C_3, the path along the line that extends from Q to the point (3,24). Thus, C'=C_1+C_2+C_3. Along the parts of C_1 and C_2 that overlap, the line integrals cancel, so we are left with the line integral over the part of C_1 that does not overlap with C_2, followed by the line integral over C_3. Thus, the line integral over C' is the same as the line integral over the direct route from the point (0,0) to the point (3,24).
(d) The parameterization (x(t),y(t)) = \left(\frac{1}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right), \frac{8}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right)\right) has (x(0),y(0)) = (0,0) and (x(3),y(3)) = (3,24). To lie along the line, we must have that y(t) = y = 8 x = 8 x(t). We can see, with a little bit of algebraic rearrangement, that the expression y(t) is in fact equal to 8\,x(t), therefore all points on the parameterized curve lie on the line y = 8 x which is the curve C.
We can find the points at which the particle changes direction by looking for where x'(t) (and y'(t)) change sign. We have x(t) = \frac{1}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right), so that x'(t) = \frac{1}{27}\left(48\,t^2 - 144\,t + 99\right). Setting this equal to zero and solving for t using the quadratic formula, we have t = \frac{3}{2} \pm \frac{1}{8}\sqrt{3}.
(e) Using the parameterization given in part (d), we have \vec r'(t)=x'(t)\vec i+y'(t)\vec j= \frac{1}{27}\left(48\,t^2 - 144\,t + 99\right)\,\vec i + \frac{8}{27}\left(48\,t^2 - 144\,t + 99\right)\,\vec j. Thus, \int_{C'} \vec{F} \cdot d\vec{r} = \int_0^{3} \vec{F}(\frac{1}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right),\frac{8}{27}\left(16\,t^3 - 72\,t^2 + 99\,t\right)) \cdot (\frac{1}{27}\left(48\,t^2 - 144\,t + 99\right)\,\vec i+ \frac{8}{27}\left(48\,t^2 - 144\,t + 99\right)\,\vec j )\,dt, which is, after expanding the dot product and simplifying, \int_0^{3} \frac{8}{19683}(48t^2 - 144 t + 99)(16t^3 - 72 t^2 + 99 t)^2 + \frac{8}{243}(48t^2 - 144 t + 99)(16t^3 - 72 t^2 + 99 t)\,dt. Numerical integration yields an answer of 180 which agrees with the answer found in part b.
